text: I think the main thing that the opposition side failed to provide is that they provide the form of the qualification but did not provide the content of the qualification. They say it's about teacher training, like having a degree or having some credits, and also maybe a test or something, but they didn't provide that what do the teachers learn in those courses, in those training, in those tests. We believe that the content has different level, for example, when you're in your high school, your teacher kind of like, for example, in my Chinese class, I'm not only learning how to write, how to have some basic stuff I can work, how to write Chinese characters, how to just read a book, I also learned some cultural things, like some literature.

I think it's also generally a general qualification to become a teacher. So what I want to say is there's a different level of the content in the qualification. Some is like a basic stuff for learning a language to work, to use, to have the ability to read, like that, or the higher level is like to understand the cultural meaning or something.

But the main problem here is for those areas with high illiteracy rate is that their people, because they are illiterate, they can't work as well as people who can read, write, and the ability gap is huge. So the main purpose of those countries, and as the opposition say, this is foundational, this is emergency, they have to let those people learn some ability to read, to write, and not just to casually talk with your friends.
So, and also, I'm a little bit confused that they didn't provide the, why is it important to lower the illiteracy rate for those countries, what's the connection between, and also the impact.

They say, oh, so one of the main argument for them is that they think the teacher who passed the qualification will be more passionate, but I think it's not really that relevant because the content of the thing that you learn in teacher course, teacher degree, teacher training, it's like mainly, based on my understanding, it's not mainly about how to be passionate about your teacher, no, how to be passionate about your student. I mean, passion is not something you can train. What you can train is the content, like the content of the language, like I said, maybe that's not called content.

So, yes, they say education is like a foundational work, and it has to be taken in the long-term view, but in a long-term work, there still has some priority, which you believe it is, it is that those people who are illiterate, to learn how to read, how to write, and once they can read, they can write, they have better ability to work, and the country who is, both sides agree, which is very poor or developing country, they can get more efficient labor and have more economic growth, which is important for the country.

And so, they say the qualification in those areas is usually imperfect, but they didn't explain how do those poor countries have the qualification system, they must be learned from somewhere, right? So, and also they mentioned that the reduction that the motion say will make the qualification more imperfect, we believe that's not true, and we believe that the qualification at this system, those developing countries, those poor countries, has now, it's mainly learned from those developed countries, they have a more perfect qualification, so they learn from that and apply it in their country, but it is not really applicable for those countries, because they can't even have a meal, why do they need to learn some cultural stuff?

So, our main argument is to lower the illiteracy rate first by reducing the qualification, which means we just need those teachers have some basic reading, writing stuff, and they can teach students, they don't have to have a huge amount of cultural knowledge, because it is the main problem that the areas are facing, and they want to solve this, and as they say, it's foundational. So, yeah, that's all the reasons above, I'm proud to propose.
